title: Morning Edition
notes: Leading this morning: NATO’s response to Russian missiles coming down in Poland, Friday’s AI-led stock sell-off, an Anthropic mathematician’s unverified claim to have proved the Riemann hypothesis, Trump’s remarks on a Canada trade deal, Hong Kong’s proposed building-safety penalties and Bessent’s account of a Trump–Xi understanding on military AI. Also: the Palisades Fire verdict, GTA VI’s first-day sales, Martin Luther King Jr.’s speech draft, B.C.’s new Conservative cabinet, Stellantis, a retracted codeine study, Daniel Carr, the U.S. commission report on Hong Kong, the AIIB, the Tara expedition, deTour, Nvidia’s California subpoena, China at COP31, a detained Princeton student, Phantom Blade Zero, COP31’s deadlock, the UK–EU deals, Denmark’s accusation against Russia and Harry Kane’s injury.

Updates on earlier stories: Russia’s Nov. 20 strikes on Ukraine (Kyiv bridges, Nov 20 edition) now with the Poland incident; Anthropic (debut Nov 20, now falling with the market); the UK–EU summit (preview Nov 20, deals now announced); COP31 (draft Nov 17 and Nov 20, now in overtime); the Shenzhen summit (Nov 19–20) with Bessent’s AI remarks; Canada–U.S. trade talks (Nov 18–20); Nvidia and chips to China (Nov 14–20).

Planned or under way, not confirmed when this edition was prepared: a final COP31 text (expected Saturday, Nov. 21), Mark Rutte’s expected visit to Poland this weekend, UK legislation on the EU deals (next week), Hong Kong’s buildings bill (January), Rinderknecht’s sentencing (March 17), the court response due in Eva Yi Xie’s case (Wednesday) and the Stellantis talks (next week).

Photos appear on the lead and on 21 of 24 other stories. All are file photos except the COP31 plenary photo, which the photographer’s file description dates to Nov. 20, 2026. Text-only where no suitable openly licensed photo was found: GTA VI, Stellantis and Phantom Blade Zero.

Stories by region: U.S. 5, Canada 5, Hong Kong 5, China 5, World 5. Several stories rest on a single outlet; this is noted under each story’s sources. The Riemann hypothesis proof, the Trump–Xi military-AI “agreement” and Russia’s role in the Danish plot are claims or assessments, not established facts.
provenance: Compiled from the linked reporting, official releases and documents listed under each story; labels show whether a point is reported, an official statement, a claim, an allegation or analysis.
Source pages were opened during this morning’s research between about 6:20 AM and 6:30 AM ET on Nov 21; each check time is the logged time that page was fetched.

RTHK is Hong Kong’s government-funded broadcaster; info.gov.hk is the Hong Kong government’s site; Sixth Tone is owned by the state-backed Shanghai United Media Group. Wire copy carried by another outlet is marked with the agency’s name (AP, AFP).

Figures differ between outlets on Nvidia’s and Anthropic’s Friday falls and on how far one missile landed from the military exercise in Poland (35 km vs about 100 km); both are given. SCMP returned HTTP 403 and ESPN a bot check (HTTP 202) to automated fetches; those are access limits, not evidence of errors, and those pages are not cited.

stories.headline: NATO calls Russian missiles that came down in Poland a “grave violation”; Warsaw says it looks like a deliberate provocation
stories.deck: Two Russian missiles and a suspected jet-powered drone fell in south-eastern Poland during Russia’s huge overnight attack on Ukraine on Nov. 20, Polish officials said. No one was hurt.
stories.summary: Two Russian missiles and a suspected jet-powered drone fell in south-eastern Poland during Russia’s huge overnight attack on Ukraine on Nov. 20, Polish officials said. No one was hurt. Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said one object, a Kh-101 cruise missile, came down at Nowy Lipowiec about 50 km from the Ukrainian border; Al Jazeera reported the others fell at Rudnik nad Sanem and Molodycz. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it appeared to be “an intentional provocation”, timed to a two-week European military exercise in Poland preparing for a possible postwar mission in Ukraine. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte called it a “grave violation” of Polish airspace, and AP (via PBS) reported he was expected to visit Poland this weekend. On Nov. 21 Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski told the BBC the missiles had guidance systems, so it was “very unlikely” they had been knocked off course by Ukrainian electronic warfare. Russia had not commented, the BBC said. Separately, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told CNN that Vladimir Putin is “a killer”, after Donald Trump called the Russian leader his “friend” at the Shenzhen summit; Trump said on Nov. 20 that he “can’t speak” to whether Putin is a friend to the U.S.
stories.why: Russian weapons have strayed into NATO territory before, but this time they came down near an exercise for a postwar force in Ukraine, and Poland’s leaders are openly calling it deliberate. That makes it harder to shrug off just as U.S. envoys push peace talks. The real test is what NATO does next: Article 5, the collective-defence clause, is a political decision, and Poland also has the option of Article 4, which only triggers consultations.
stories.label: Reported + Official statement + Claim
stories.note: Accounts of distance differ: AP (via PBS) and Al Jazeera say one missile came down about 35 km from the exercise area; the BBC quotes Polish authorities as saying about 100 km. Both are given here. Russia’s intent is unconfirmed; “provocation” is the Polish government’s assessment.

stories.headline: AI sell-off sinks the S&P 500 3.7% into a correction; Nvidia falls about 14% and Anthropic gives back half its debut gain
stories.deck: The Nasdaq composite fell 5.3% on Friday, Nov. 20, and turned negative for 2026, as chip stocks led a broad retreat from AI-linked shares.
stories.summary: A sell-off in artificial-intelligence stocks pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7% on Friday, Nov. 20, putting it in a “correction” more than 10% below its Oct. 6 record, NPR reported, citing AP. The Nasdaq composite slid 5.3% and turned negative for the year; the Dow fell 1.9%. NPR said it was the S&P 500’s worst week since April 2025 and capped a seven-day losing streak. Chipmakers led the fall: AMD sank 13.3%, Micron 13.9% and Broadcom 12.1%. Nvidia closed down about 14% (13.7% to 13.8% depending on the outlet), its seventh straight weekly decline, the longest since 2008, CNBC reported, after a Reuters report, which the BBC said it had not confirmed, that the SEC is looking at its accounting. Anthropic, a day after its Nasdaq debut, fell 8.5% (BBC) to 9.1% (NPR), giving back about half its first-day gain but staying above its $83 IPO price. Japan’s Nikkei and South Korea’s Kospi each fell more than 5% overnight.
stories.why: AI stocks drove most of Wall Street’s gains this year, so their slide now drags down the whole market, including the retirement and index funds many people hold. Analysts point to doubts about the huge spending on data centres, worries over Nvidia since Jensen Huang’s exit, and November’s midterm results, which strengthened candidates who favour tighter rules on data centres. One bad week isn’t a crash, but the market is now asking whether AI spending will pay off.
stories.label: Reported + Analysis
stories.note: Figures differ slightly between outlets for Nvidia (13.7%–14%) and Anthropic (8.5%–9.1%); ranges are given.

stories.headline: Anthropic mathematician says he used Claude to prove the Riemann hypothesis; experts say checking it will take a long time
stories.deck: Levent Alpöge says an unreleased version of Claude helped him produce a proof of maths’ most famous unsolved problem, more than 250,000 pages long. It has not been verified.
stories.summary: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician on Anthropic’s technical staff, said on Friday, Nov. 20, that over about six weeks he used a non-public version of the company’s Claude chatbot to produce a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, the BBC and DW reported. The 1859 conjecture about how prime numbers are distributed is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute’s seven Millennium Prize Problems, each carrying a $1 million prize. Alpöge wrote that the work generated more than 250,000 pages, written in the proof-checking language Lean, and that he had not yet mastered all the mathematics involved. He also acknowledged the announcement came a day after Anthropic’s stock-market debut, calling the timing “horrible” and rejecting a cynical reading. Mathematician Terence Tao said verification is still some way off. Clay Institute president Martin Bridson, quoted by AP via DW, called it “an announcement of historic significance” but said “the journey… to a place of real understanding will be long and difficult.”
stories.why: If the proof holds, it would be one of the biggest results in the history of mathematics and the strongest evidence yet that AI can do original research at the very top level. Until other mathematicians check it, though, it is a claim, and one that is unusually hard to check. Its timing, right after Anthropic’s IPO, means people will also scrutinise the motives behind it.
stories.label: Claim + Reported
stories.note: The proof is unverified. “Solved” in some headlines goes further than the sources: the BBC says the claim would be significant “if found to be correct”.

stories.headline: Jury convicts Los Angeles man of starting the fire that grew into the deadly 2025 Palisades Fire
stories.deck: Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, was found guilty of two federal charges at a retrial on Friday, Nov. 20, after his first trial ended with a deadlocked jury in June.
stories.summary: A federal jury in Los Angeles on Friday, Nov. 20, convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, of starting a fire on Jan. 1, 2025, that smouldered in root systems and flared up again on Jan. 7 to become the Palisades Fire, one of the most destructive wildfires in California history. It killed 12 people and destroyed more than 6,800 buildings in Pacific Palisades and Malibu, the BBC reported. He was convicted on both counts, one for the original Lachman Fire and one for the Palisades Fire, AP (via PBS) reported. His first trial in June ended in a mistrial after jurors deadlocked 10-2 in favour of acquittal. At the retrial, prosecutors relied on phone location data, photos of his car near the trail, fire-camera images and witness testimony. His lawyers said they were disappointed but respected the verdict. Sentencing is scheduled for March 17; he faces five to 20 years on each charge.
stories.why: For families who lost homes and relatives, the verdict brings a measure of accountability nearly two years later. Many of them are still trying to rebuild, and arguments over how Los Angeles prepared for and handled the fires go on.
stories.label: Reported + Official statement

stories.headline: Grand Theft Auto VI took in $3.79 billion on its first day, Rockstar says, calling it the biggest entertainment launch ever
stories.deck: The figure is the publisher’s own estimate of worldwide retail sales through the end of launch day, Nov. 19.
stories.summary: Rockstar Games, part of New York-based Take-Two Interactive, said on Friday, Nov. 20, that Grand Theft Auto VI brought in $3.79 billion in day-one retail sales, based on company estimates through the end of Nov. 19, the day it launched. It called that a record for any entertainment product. The company also said the game sold 32.5 million units before release, a record across platforms, and has a Metacritic score of 99. According to AFP (via RTHK), that is nearly five times what Grand Theft Auto V took in during its first 24 hours in 2013. The game is out on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, after more than eight years in development and two delays.
stories.why: It shows how big video games now are as entertainment: by the company’s count, one game’s opening day beat any film or album launch. The number comes from Rockstar and hasn’t been independently audited, but it sets expectations for Take-Two’s next earnings and for the industry.

stories.headline: Martin Luther King Jr.’s handwritten draft of the “I Have a Dream” speech goes on public display for the first time
stories.deck: The seven-page draft, the only one known, is on show at Atlanta’s National Center for Civil and Human Rights through Sunday. It doesn’t include the words “I have a dream.”
stories.summary: The only known draft of Martin Luther King Jr.’s 1963 March on Washington speech, handwritten in blue ink on yellow legal paper, is on public display for the first time at the National Center for Civil and Human Rights in Atlanta, NPR reported on Nov. 20. The seven-page manuscript shows King crossing out whole sections and reworking phrases. According to the centre’s CEO, Jill Savitt, King originally titled it “Normalcy Never Again”, and the draft doesn’t contain the famous “I have a dream” lines, which he improvised on the day. NPR said the document will be on exhibit through Sunday.
stories.why: It is a rare look at how one of the most famous speeches in U.S. history was actually written: drafted, crossed out and rewritten, with the best-remembered lines improvised in front of the crowd. Anyone who works with spoken text can see the gap between the page and the performance.
stories.label: Reported
stories.note: Single outlet (NPR). Display dates as reported by NPR.

stories.headline: Trump says he is working on a “fair” trade deal with Canada but that “more work remains”
stories.deck: At a White House news conference on Nov. 20, Trump praised Carney and his Keystone pipeline pitch, but repeated familiar complaints about Canadian trade.
stories.summary: Speaking at a White House news conference on Friday, Nov. 20, after his Asia trip, which included a brief meeting with Prime Minister Mark Carney, U.S. President Donald Trump said “we’re working on making a deal that’s fair” with Canada, while adding that “more work remains to be done.” He said Carney wants to build a Keystone pipeline for the U.S. — “we like that. But, you know, got to do a lot more than that.” Trump repeated claims that Canada has been ripping off the U.S. and put the trade deficit at “about $80 billion”; CBC noted the actual 2025 U.S. goods deficit with Canada was $48 billion US. “When it’s down to zero, come over and let’s start talking,” he said. Ottawa is seeking an interim deal to remove the 50% tariffs imposed in August and ease sectoral tariffs on steel, aluminum, autos and lumber, and hoping to head off Trump’s threat to raise auto tariffs to 50% on Jan. 1, which has not been formally filed, CBC reported.
stories.why: Trump sounds warmer about a deal than he did a few weeks ago, but he hasn’t moved on the substance, and the Jan. 1 auto-tariff threat is six weeks away. For Canada’s auto, steel and forestry towns, what matters is whether an interim deal arrives before then, not how friendly the meetings are.
stories.label: Official statement + Claim + Reported
stories.note: Single outlet. Trump’s trade-deficit figure is his claim; CBC gives the 2025 goods deficit as $48 billion US.

stories.headline: Lorne Doerkson sworn in as B.C. premier with the province’s first Conservative cabinet
stories.deck: The new premier’s smaller cabinet has 18 ministers and six ministers of state, and housing is no longer a stand-alone ministry.
stories.summary: Lorne Doerkson was sworn in as British Columbia’s 38th premier on Friday, Nov. 20, alongside the first B.C. Conservative cabinet, at Government House in Victoria, CBC News reported. The Conservatives won the province’s largest majority in 25 years in a snap election called by former NDP premier David Eby; 63 Conservative MLAs were sworn in on Thursday, with one more pending a judicial recount next week. Doerkson’s cabinet is smaller than the NDP’s 23 ministries: 18 ministers, six ministers of state and 12 parliamentary secretaries. Housing and infrastructure are no longer stand-alone ministries, and red-tape reduction is a new ministry of state. Claire Rattée, a former Kitimat councillor who has spoken about her experience with addiction in Vancouver’s Downtown Eastside, is deputy premier. Doerkson promised to be transparent and admit mistakes.
stories.why: It is a big political shift in a province long run by the NDP, and the new cabinet’s shape (fewer ministries, housing folded into others, a red-tape ministry) shows where the government says it will focus. How it handles housing costs and the overdose crisis will be early tests.
stories.label: Reported + Official statement
stories.note: Single outlet.

stories.headline: Stellantis would owe Ottawa about $831 million if its Brampton plant sale goes ahead, a federal source tells CBC
stories.deck: After a meeting on Nov. 20 with the automaker, Ottawa and Unifor, Premier Doug Ford called the talks “challenging” but “productive” and blamed tariffs and emissions rules.
stories.summary: Stellantis would owe the federal government about $831 million if it sells its Brampton, Ont., assembly plant, a senior federal source told CBC News on Friday, Nov. 20, after Ontario Premier Doug Ford put the figure at “roughly” $873 million. The company met Ford, federal Industry Minister Mélanie Joly and union officials in Toronto after confirming the planned sale of the plant to armoured-vehicle maker Roshel. Ottawa has threatened to sue over support given under a 2022 agreement; the company has offered to repay $24 million. Ford said the company told them U.S. tariffs and greenhouse-gas standards make the plant unviable, and that keeping it “open and warm” without production costs about $135 million a year, Global News reported. Unifor’s Lana Payne called the emissions standards an “irritant”. Talks are to continue next week.
stories.why: Auto jobs in Brampton and Canada’s bargaining position with the U.S. are both tied up in this plant. Figures are being reported through a source and a premier, not an official public accounting. The dispute also pits Ottawa’s climate rules against keeping auto plants open, which is a hard trade-off for any government.
stories.label: Reported + Unnamed sources + Official statement
stories.note: The $831 million figure comes from an unnamed federal source; Ford’s figure is $873 million.

stories.headline: The Lancet retracts a 2006 Toronto study that blamed a baby’s death on codeine in breast milk, citing “falsification”
stories.deck: The case report by Motherisk founder Gideon Koren shaped breastfeeding and pain-relief guidance worldwide for two decades.
stories.summary: The Lancet has retracted a 2006 case report by Gideon Koren, founder of the Motherisk lab at Toronto’s Hospital for Sick Children (SickKids), which linked an Ontario baby’s 2005 death to codeine passed through his mother’s breast milk, CBC News reported on Nov. 21. The journal said omissions in the research amounted to “falsification”, after receiving the outcome of an investigation by SickKids’ research-integrity office. The paper had carried an “expression of concern” since February, following new allegations about falsified toxicology data, authorship and ethics. Critics such as Toronto pharmacologist Dr. David Juurlink say the study led many women who were taking opioids after childbirth to give up breastfeeding.
stories.why: This one disputed case report helped set global advice for new mothers for 20 years. Its retraction may lead to a rethink of how opioid pain relief and breastfeeding are handled after birth, and it is a reminder that a single case report can carry far more weight than it should.
stories.label: Reported + Official statement
stories.note: Single outlet. Koren’s side is not set out in the CBC report as checked; the retraction notice says he was unlikely to be able to participate meaningfully in the investigation.

stories.headline: Swiss prosecutors open a criminal case against ex-NHL forward Daniel Carr over a punch to a downed opponent
stories.deck: The Alberta-born HC Ajoie forward is suspected of attempted serious assault after an Oct. 16 game in which Biel captain Gaetan Haas was concussed.
stories.summary: Swiss prosecutors have opened criminal proceedings against former NHL forward Daniel Carr, 35, of Sherwood Park, Alta., on suspicion of attempted serious assault, CBC Sports reported. Prosecutors say the HC Ajoie forward punched EHC Biel-Bienne captain Gaetan Haas in the head while Haas was down on the ice during an Oct. 16 National League game; Biel says Haas suffered a concussion. Prosecutors said on Friday, Nov. 20, that they opened the case on Oct. 23, partly on the basis of live TV footage, and that police have interviewed both players. The Swiss federation raised Carr’s suspension from five to seven games and his fine to 9,040 Swiss francs. Carr played 117 NHL games for Montreal, Vegas, Nashville and Washington.
stories.why: Criminal charges for on-ice violence are rare, so this case could matter well beyond Switzerland in deciding where hockey discipline ends and the criminal law begins. Carr has not been charged with or convicted of a crime; prosecutors have opened an investigation.
stories.label: Reported + Allegation
stories.note: Single outlet. An investigation, not a conviction.

stories.headline: Hong Kong proposes fines of up to HK$10 million and five years’ jail for building works that cause death or injury, after the Wang Fuk Court fire
stories.deck: The plans would require permits for large-scale maintenance projects. Separately, the chief secretary said lawful memorials for the fire’s 168 victims are “absolutely permitted”.
stories.summary: Hong Kong’s Development Bureau has proposed tightening the Buildings Ordinance after last November’s Wang Fuk Court fire in Tai Po, RTHK reported on Nov. 20. Large-scale maintenance works, on buildings of four storeys or more with scaffolding covering a whole side across at least four floors, would no longer count as minor works: they would need a Buildings Department permit, prescribed plans and a supervision plan. Works that cause or may cause death, injury or property damage would become a new offence with maximum penalties of HK$10 million and five years in prison, up from HK$1 million and three years. Using substandard materials could bring HK$3 million and three years. Contractors found to have engaged in bribery or bid-rigging could be struck off registers for three years without a disciplinary hearing. The region holds about a third of the world’s coral reefs, and its coral cover has held steady while as much as half of the world’s reefs were lost over four decades, according to the report. stories.summary: Bayern Munich said England captain Harry Kane tore the syndesmosis ligament in his left ankle during Friday’s 1-1 Bundesliga draw with Cologne and “will therefore be out for the next few months,” Al Jazeera reported. Kane, 33, was caught by a Cologne defender’s follow-through after about 20 minutes and limped off with physiotherapists. He became the first Englishman in 25 years to win the Ballon d’Or last month and recently signed a contract keeping him at Bayern until June 2029. The night also marked coach Vincent Kompany’s return to the dugout a month after he collapsed while watching a reserve-team training session.
stories.why: Kane has scored 156 goals in 161 games for Bayern, so losing him for months hits both the club’s title push and England’s plans, with the timing of his return still unclear.
